preview.name: strip-ansi
preview.description: strip-ansi is a small string-processing library for removing ANSI escape codes from text. Its README describes that purpose; the implementation returns a string with matches from ansi-regex removed.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body:
A representative call is stripAnsi('\u009B31mfoo\u009B39m'): a string containing color codes introduced by the 8-bit CSI character around the text “foo.” The test suite passes this exact input to the exported function.

The function first checks that its argument is a string, throwing a TypeError otherwise. It returns immediately only when neither ESC (\u001B) nor CSI (\u009B) occurs. This input contains CSI, so it continues to the replacement step.

At module initialization, ansiRegex() creates a shared regex. For the example input, stripAnsi reaches string.replace(regex, ''), replacing matched escape sequences with empty text rather than modifying the visible text deliberately.

The test asserts that this call returns 'foo': the color-control sequences are gone and the enclosed text remains.

sections.title: A closer look
sections.body:
A meaningful optimization is the introducer check: ordinary strings avoid regex replacement altogether. Tests assert that both 'foo bar' and the empty string are returned unchanged.

The implementation deliberately does not reset the shared regex's lastIndex. Its comment explains that replace handles this automatically for a global regex, unlike exec or test, and that manually resetting it has a performance penalty.

The library exposes an ES-module entry at index.js and a TypeScript declaration at index.d.ts. The declared API is a default function accepting a string and returning a string.

sections.title: Where to look next
sections.body:
To explore behavior beyond color removal, read test.js's terminal-link and OSC cases. They assert that a terminal hyperlink becomes 'click' and that an OSC-containing input retains 'ABC\r\n', giving concrete examples of which text should survive stripping.

For questions about exactly which escape sequences match, follow ansi-regex, which the README identifies as the escape-code matching regex and index.js imports directly. For local validation work, package.json defines the test script as 'xo && ava && tsd'.
